title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Pond and water-feature maintenance
audience: Owners of small Australian pond and water-feature maintenance businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short visits, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A pond rate depends on the owner's skill with pumps, filters and water chemistry, the range of water features served, whether fish are part of the job, the scale of each system, and how much travel the route needs. An owner who can offer a visit, a filter clean and a seasonal check in one trip may justify a higher rate, because the client saves time. Local evidence is the weak point for this course. No pond or water-feature price with a stated figure was found in the research, and the cost-guide sites that appeared in search were not opened. Do not use a national average. Build the rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with competitors' published prices, checking that each one is insured and licensed for the work.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel, quoting, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract the non-billable time to reach billable hours. Jobber's general guidance puts billable time at about 60 to 80 percent of working hours, but that is a general range and not an Australian figure, so check your own log against it. For example, if seventy of every hundred paid hours are billable (illustrative), the costs of all one hundred hours must be recovered from the seventy.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, registration, equipment and its upkeep, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income needed to live on. Business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure. Decide how each will be allowed for, and have a registered tax agent confirm the treatment for the owner's situation before the rate is published (1 October 2026). Divide the total by the billable hours to reach the base rate. Xero Australia uses the same approach, working from take-home pay, business costs and super. Its example gives about $81 an hour, but that example is not a pond rate. Review the base rate each quarter.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short visits
instruction.body: A short pond visit can cost more in travel and set-up than it earns, because the drive to the site and the set-up do not shrink with the size of the task. A minimum charge or call-out fee covers the time needed to attend the site. Set the minimum so that a short visit still covers travel, set-up and admin. Contractor+ suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, dividing that cost by one minus the target margin. Its figures are labelled illustrative by the source: a $105 visit cost at a 30 percent target margin gives a $150 minimum. Price several small tasks at one visit as one labour amount, not as a separate minimum for each task, and price any extra work before starting it. State the minimum before the visit and explain it in plain words.

instruction.heading: Review and raise the rate
instruction.body: Business Victoria recommends reviewing prices about every three months, and checking that they still suit the business and its customers (undated page). Give existing clients written notice of any change, and honour quotes that were already approved at the old rate.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a short visit, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: An owner's calculation shows that only seventy of every hundred paid hours can be billed (illustrative). The owner plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pricing as if every paid hour were billable understates the rate, because the costs and the income still have to come out of the hours that can be billed. At a 70 per cent billable share (illustrative), the rate must be about 1.43 times the rate needed for a fully billable week (1 divided by 0.7). The rate must be built from billable hours, then checked against the owner's competitor evidence and the minimum charge before it is published.

equipmentAndPpe: Log of paid and billable hours for one month
Price sheet with the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published average or a competitor's figure without checking the costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from the owner's own costs and billable hours, then compare it with the competitor evidence that you have checked.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time, including travel, before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short visits at the same rate, without covering travel and set-up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited (setting prices: what's allowed, 15 July 2026). The ACCC page cited here does not settle minimum or call-out charges, so check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.

Do not price work you are not permitted to do. Moving koi needs a permit in Victoria, and releasing fish is illegal in New South Wales without a permit. Do not include fish relocation or release in a rate or minimum charge until the rule for the state has been checked. No pond licence requirement was confirmed in any state.
Confirm the tax treatment of leave, superannuation and the owner's own income with a registered tax agent before publishing the rate.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with checked local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short visits.

knowledgeChecks.question: A pond owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per visit
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for short pond visits?
options: Because short visits need travel but no set-up time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, set-up and admin time does not shrink with the size of the visit
Because clients expect every visit to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate for a pond business?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with checked local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure; going-rate pricing is one approach.

Xero Australia, 'How to price services', https://www.xero.com/au/guides/how-to-price-services/, dated 3 September 2026. Supports: rate from take-home pay, business costs and super divided by billable hours. The page's example is not a pond rate.

Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. General range, not an Australian figure. Supports: billable time typically 60 to 80 percent of working hours.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. The source labels its figures illustrative, not market rates. Supports: minimum set from the full visit cost divided by one minus target margin; the minimum covers travel, set-up and admin.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Victoria. Supports: review prices about every three months; competitors' prices are not to be assumed right.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

Queensland Department of Agriculture and Fisheries, 'Ipa aquarium fish importation' fact sheet, https://www.daf.qld.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0004/1457824/ipa-aquarium-fish-importation.pdf, dated June 2020. Supports: fish must not be released into waterways, wetlands or drains.

Victorian Fisheries Authority, 'Noxious aquatic species in Victoria', https://vfa.vic.gov.au/operational-policy/pests-and-diseases/noxious-aquatic-species-in-victoria, undated. Supports: koi carp need a permit to keep, transport or possess.

NSW DPI, 'Freshwater pest fish in NSW', Primefact 1336, https://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0010/637129/Primefact-1336-Freshwater-pest-fish-in-NSW.pdf, September 2023. Supports: releasing fish into NSW public waters without a permit is illegal.

Gap: no pond or water-feature minimum or call-out charge from a trade or government source was found. No pond price with a stated figure was opened. No Australian pond trade-body source was reached. Minimum-charge rules for Australian pond work were not confirmed.
